pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–12 years

- **Topic:** Drawing Force Diagrams

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, KS3 Physics — Forces):** Using force arrows in diagrams, adding forces in 1 dimension, balanced and unbalanced forces (the formal arrow representation; informal force arrows are introduced earlier across KS2 forces).

- **Standards — US (NGSS — no discrete elementary PE; relates to 3-PS2-1 / MS-PS2-2):** Balanced and unbalanced forces are assessed at 3-PS2-1 and force-sum reasoning at MS-PS2-2; the formal free-body diagram convention is introduced at HS-PS2.

- **Operational details:** This is a REPRESENTATIONAL skill spanning ages 7-12: representing forces as labelled arrows on an object, where the arrow's LENGTH shows the force's size and its DIRECTION shows which way the force acts. Pupils show multiple forces on one object, read the diagram to decide whether forces are BALANCED (equal arrows in opposite directions, no resultant, no change in motion) or UNBALANCED (unequal arrows, a resultant that speeds up, slows, or turns the object), and draw the resultant as a single arrow. The disciplined habit to instil is the free-body / 'replacement principle': pick ONE object and draw only the forces acting ON it, with arrow tails attached to the object (not floating in mid-air) and each arrow labelled by force type. For younger pupils it is a relative diagram, not a precise scale drawing.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal).
bestPractices: Draw ONE body at a time: start from a situation with NO arrows, then add only the forces acting on the chosen object (the replacement principle), repeating per object if several interact.
Attach every arrow's tail to the object and label it by force type — explicitly avoid 'arrows hanging in mid-air' and ambiguity about which object a force acts on.
Use the physical 'cardboard arrows' manipulative (IOP, 5-11) to build diagrams before drawing them on paper.
Use arrow LENGTH for relative magnitude (longer = bigger); treat it as a diagram, not a strict scale drawing, for younger learners — prioritise correct direction and attachment.

Teach explicitly that BALANCED forces does not mean 'no forces' and does not necessarily mean 'stationary' — it can mean moving at constant speed; confront this with a coasting/constant-velocity case drawn with equal opposing arrows.
Always link the diagram to a prediction of motion ('what will the object do?') so the arrows mean something physical.
keyRepresentations: The labelled force arrow (length = magnitude, direction = way it acts)
IOP 'cardboard arrows' physical manipulative for building diagrams
Single-object free-body diagram (other objects 'replaced' by arrows on the chosen body)
The resultant arrow (single arrow summarising the net force)
commonMisconceptions: Drawing arrows 'hanging in mid-air', detached from the object, or unclear which object a force acts on (so it's impossible to tell push-of-A-on-B from B-on-A).
Motion implies a force: drawing a forward force arrow on anything that is moving, even at constant velocity (impetus).
Confusing the direction of velocity with the direction of the net force (Viennot's juggler task — persists after instruction).
Believing balanced forces must mean the object is stationary (not realising constant-velocity motion also has balanced forces).
Ignoring arrow length (all arrows drawn the same), or over-demanding an exact scale that obscures the physics for young learners.
Reading the diagram as a literal picture of the scene rather than as a representation of vector forces.

learn.summary: Learners aged 7-12 build and interpret force diagrams: forces shown as labelled arrows on one chosen object, where arrow LENGTH shows relative size and DIRECTION shows which way the force acts. They use diagrams to decide whether forces are balanced (equal, opposite arrows, no resultant) or unbalanced (unequal arrows, a resultant), draw a single resultant arrow, and link the diagram to a prediction of motion. The core habit to instil is the free-body / replacement principle: pick ONE object and draw only the forces acting ON it, with arrow tails attached to the body (not floating in mid-air) and each arrow labelled by force type. Key conceptual targets include that balanced forces do not mean 'no forces' and do not necessarily mean 'stationary' (constant-velocity coasting also has balanced forces), that a resultant force determines how an object's motion CHANGES (its acceleration) relative to how it is already moving, and that motion does not require a forward force.

activities.title: Arrow editor: forces that drive the crate
feedback: If arrows are equal and opposite, state that forces are balanced: no resultant, so no change in motion — the crate either stays at rest or keeps moving at the same steady speed it already had.

If one arrow is longer, name the resultant's direction, then describe the change relative to the crate's current motion: it speeds up if already moving that way, slows if moving the opposite way, or turns if the resultant is sideways.
If an arrow floats away from the crate, prompt: every arrow's tail starts ON the crate and shows a force acting ON it — one body at a time.

On the coasting challenge, state the friction model first. Assume negligible horizontal friction: the gliding crate needs NO horizontal arrows at all (only the vertical weight-down and support-up pair, which balance), and it keeps gliding at steady speed with zero net force. If a learner adds a forward push, do not reject it just because the crate is moving — ask what balances it: with no friction nothing does, so the crate would speed up. (If the model instead has appreciable friction, a forward push exactly balanced by backward friction keeps constant speed; the net force is still zero.) Either way, no NET forward force is required to keep moving.
activities.rationale: Editing arrows and observing the resulting motion makes balanced-vs-unbalanced a felt cause and gives a concrete way to confront the impetus misconception that moving things need a forward force. Live coupling between arrow and motion lets the learner test how changing an arrow changes the motion (an affordance of the interactive, not a claim that static images cannot teach the concept).
sourceClaims: 'Motion implies force' is the most-reported force misconception (K-12 and college); students conflate the direction of velocity with the direction of net force (Viennot's juggler task), a confusion pervasive even after instruction.

A free-body diagram is a diagram of ONE object with other objects replaced by forces on it (replacement principle); a common flaw is arrows 'hanging in mid-air' making it unclear which object a force acts on; arrow length encodes relative magnitude but it is a diagram, not a scaled drawing; teach one body at a time starting from a no-arrows situation.
learnerActions: Start from a crate with NO arrows drawn on it.

Add force arrows to the crate; set each arrow's length and direction (for example by dragging a handle at the arrow's tip), with every arrow's tail locked to the crate — only forces acting ON the crate are allowed.
Make two opposing arrows equal in length and predict, then check, what the crate does; then make one arrow longer and predict/check again, stating the crate's current motion each time.
Read or draw the resultant as a single arrow summarising the net force.

Attempt the 'coasting' challenge: a crate is already sliding to the right on a surface with negligible horizontal friction — decide what arrows (if any) it needs to keep gliding at steady speed, then test it.
Label each arrow by force type (e.g. push, friction, weight, support).
activities.intendedInsight: The arrows cause the CHANGE in motion (the acceleration): equal opposing arrows give no change (an object stays still if it was still, or keeps gliding at constant speed if it was already moving), while unequal arrows give a resultant whose direction determines how the motion changes — a box already moving the resultant's way speeds up, a box moving the opposite way first slows. A still-moving crate kept at steady speed with no net forward force overturns 'motion needs a forward force'.

activities.title: Cardboard arrows: build the diagram by hand first
feedback: Check each arrow's tail touches the object — a piece lying away from the object has no clear owner.
If both pieces are the same length when the forces differ, ask which force should be bigger and swap in a longer piece.
When two objects interact, confirm the learner has drawn only the forces on the single chosen object, not forces that object exerts on others.
activities.rationale: A hands-on manipulative supports younger learners in identifying the forces acting on each object before the drawing convention is formalised; this is offered as a bridge to paper diagrams, not as the only route to the skill.
sourceClaims: Many students cannot correctly identify the forces acting on each object when two or more objects interact, so they struggle to construct accurate free-body diagrams; the recommended primary manipulative is 'cardboard arrows' (5-11) to build up force diagrams, plus a 'describing interactions' framework.

A free-body diagram is a diagram of ONE object with other objects replaced by forces on it (replacement principle); a common flaw is arrows 'hanging in mid-air' making it unclear which object a force acts on; arrow length encodes relative magnitude but it is a diagram, not a scaled drawing; teach one body at a time starting from a no-arrows situation.
learnerActions: Use physical 'cardboard arrows' (cut to different lengths) laid onto a picture or model of one object to build up its force diagram before drawing on paper.
Place each arrow so its tail sits on the object and point it the way the force acts; pick a longer piece for a bigger force.
For a pair of interacting objects, build the diagram for ONE object at a time, replacing the other object with the force arrow it exerts.
Describe out loud which object each arrow acts on and name the force type.
activities.intendedInsight: A force diagram is a representation of one chosen object with the forces acting ON it; building it physically makes the replacement principle and arrow attachment concrete before committing to pencil.

activities.title: Interpret and construct: the resting book and the pushed box
feedback: Box: the arrows are opposite and the push is longer, so forces are unbalanced with a resultant to the right — and because the box is already moving right, it speeds up.
Resting book: draw two arrows ON the book — weight DOWN and the table's support force UP — equal in length (balanced), both starting on the book, so it stays still.
If nothing is drawn on the book: a still book has weight down and the table pushing up, equal and opposite — balanced does not mean absent.
If only the weight is drawn: the table also pushes up on the book; without it the book would not stay still.
Equal push and friction → balanced → no change in motion, so the box keeps moving right at the steady speed it already had.

Friction longer than push → resultant to the left → the rightward-moving box slows down and comes to a stop. It does NOT reverse: sliding (kinetic) friction only opposes the box's current rightward slip, so it cannot by itself drive the box backward. Once the box stops, reassess the forces: kinetic friction no longer acts, but the rightward push is still present and is now balanced by static friction, so the box stays at rest rather than reversing or re-accelerating. Reversal would need a sustained non-friction force pushing left.
activities.rationale: Mixing interpretation (read direction and length) with construction (translate a situation into arrows attached to and acting on one object) surfaces the specific misconceptions — floating arrows, 'still = no forces', and ignoring length as magnitude — and requires the learner to produce a diagram, not only recognise one.
sourceClaims: A free-body diagram is a diagram of ONE object with other objects replaced by forces on it (replacement principle); a common flaw is arrows 'hanging in mid-air' making it unclear which object a force acts on; arrow length encodes relative magnitude but it is a diagram, not a scaled drawing; teach one body at a time starting from a no-arrows situation.
learnerActions: Look at a force diagram of a box being pushed to the right across the floor (already moving right): a long arrow right labelled 'push' and a shorter arrow left labelled 'friction'. State what the lengths and directions tell you about what the box is doing.
Identify the resultant's direction and justify it from the arrow lengths.
Draw the force arrows for a book resting still on a table, attaching each arrow to the book and labelling it.
Redraw the box with push and friction EQUAL and say what the box is now doing.
Answer: if the friction arrow became longer than the push, what would happen to the box that is moving right?
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a diagram: the longer opposing arrow sets the resultant's direction → unbalanced → the motion changes that way relative to how the box is already moving. Constructing a diagram: even a still object has forces — weight down AND the table's support (normal) force up, equal and opposite (balanced), both starting on the book — so 'still' is drawn with balanced arrows, not a blank.

activities.title: Spot the error / match the motion (quick checks)
feedback: Reject 'must be stationary' when the object is already moving: balanced forces mean no change in motion, which includes constant-speed gliding.
For a mid-air arrow, reattach its tail to the object and confirm which object the force acts on.

When identifying the resultant, confirm it points in the direction of the net force and is drawn as a single arrow. For two opposite arrows, that is the way of the longer arrow. For several arrows along one line, add up the arrows pointing each way and compare the totals; the longest single arrow does not always win. Then state how the resultant changes the object's motion relative to how it is already moving.
activities.rationale: Short targeted items check and reinforce the conventions and can expose the named misconceptions; recognition-style items check interpretation and should be paired with at least one construction (draw/sketch) item, since selecting an answer does not itself elicit independent diagram construction.
learnerActions: Error-finding: given a diagram, spot the arrow that does not start on the object ('spot the mid-air arrow') and redraw it correctly.
Choose from outcomes for 'balanced or unbalanced — what happens next?', including a 'must be stationary' option to be rejected when the object is already moving.
Match each diagram to its motion description.
Identify the resultant for a given pair or set of arrows.
Sketch the arrows onto a pictured object for a described situation, stating the object's current motion.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent learners consistently attach arrows to the object, read length as magnitude and direction as the way the force acts, and know balanced forces can accompany steady motion, not only rest.

constraints: For learners aged 7-12 treat the diagram as a relative diagram, not a strict scale drawing: prioritise correct direction and attachment, with longer = bigger, rather than exact scaling that can obscure the physics.
Always enforce the replacement principle: one chosen object, only the forces acting ON it, every arrow's tail attached to the body, each arrow labelled by force type.

A static annotated gallery (tap an arrow for its meaning, tap for the balanced/unbalanced verdict and outcome) is useful reading and recap practice but does not let the learner test how changing an arrow changes the motion; use it as a companion, not the primary construction task.
A multiple-choice/recognition item assesses interpretation but does not by itself elicit independent construction of a diagram; include at least one draw/sketch task.

When describing changes in motion, state the object's current motion: a resultant (unbalanced) force determines ACCELERATION — it changes motion (speeds up, slows, or turns) RELATIVE to how the object is already moving, not the instantaneous direction of travel. Balanced forces mean no change in motion, which may be rest OR constant-velocity gliding.

In the coasting case, declare the friction model explicitly. With negligible horizontal friction a gliding object needs no horizontal arrows (only the balanced vertical weight/support pair); with appreciable friction a forward push balanced by backward friction keeps constant speed. Do not reject a learner's forward push merely because the object is moving — ask what balances friction in the stated model.

Kinetic (sliding) friction opposes an object's current slip: it can slow a sliding box to rest but cannot keep acting in one direction to reverse it. When a sliding object stops, reassess the forces — kinetic friction no longer applies, but static friction may balance a continuing applied push so the object stays at rest. Only a sustained non-friction applied force can reverse the direction of travel.
Physical cardboard arrows and a screen-based arrow editor offer different experiences; the manipulative is a bridge for younger learners and neither is presented as universally necessary.

Force diagrams use a deliberately planar 2D convention; a flat representation matches the skill being taught. (This is a fit note, not a claim that 3D rendering can never support any related learning.)
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Of the three cited sources, the IOP/cardboard-arrows claim is marked verified in the source row; the free-body/replacement-principle claim and the 'motion implies force'/Viennot claim are marked unverified. Do not treat legacy confidence as fresh verification.

The original 'ideal' entry asserted the live editor 'directly defeats' the impetus misconception and that 'live state is essential'. These comparative-efficacy/necessity claims are not established by the cited sources; softened here to a stated affordance (live coupling lets the learner test arrow→motion) without a necessity claim.

The original 'poor' ratings for 3D and conversation included universal-sounding claims ('rendering in 3D undermines the very representation', dialogue 'offers no efficient route'). These are not established by the sources and have been reduced to narrowly scoped fit notes.

Audit of the worked example: for a box already moving right with push (right, long) and friction (left, short), resultant is to the right and the box speeds up — consistent. For the resting book, weight down and support up, equal and opposite, balanced — consistent. The 'friction longer than push' case is corrected so the rightward-moving box decelerates to a stop and does NOT reverse: kinetic friction only opposes the current rightward slip. Once stopped, kinetic friction ceases but the still-present rightward push is balanced by static friction, so the box remains at rest; reversal would require a sustained non-friction force to the left.

The coasting challenge declares its friction model (default negligible horizontal friction, with the appreciable-friction alternative noted) so that a learner's forward push is questioned against what balances friction rather than rejected for the object being in motion.

probeDeeper: In the box diagram, which way is the resultant force, and how did the arrow lengths tell you?
For your resting book — which object is each arrow acting ON? Point to where each arrow starts.
Draw the arrows for the same box when the push and friction are EQUAL. What is the box doing now?
If I made the friction arrow longer than the push, what would happen to the box?
assess.correctAnswer: The two arrows are opposite (push right, friction left) and the push arrow is LONGER, so the forces are unbalanced with a resultant to the right — the box speeds up / moves right. For the resting book: two arrows ON the book — weight pointing DOWN and the table's support (normal) force pointing UP — equal in length (balanced), both starting on the book, so it stays still.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'A still object has no forces, so I'll draw no arrows.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: A still book has weight down AND the table pushing up, equal and opposite; balanced does not mean absent.
errorPatterns.distractor: Nothing is happening to the book, so there are no forces to draw.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Draws nothing on the resting book, or only the weight arrow.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Arrows can float anywhere near the object.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Every arrow starts ON the object and shows a force acting ON it — one body at a time (the replacement principle).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Draws arrows not starting on the object, or is unclear which object each force acts on.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The arrow's length doesn't mean anything — you read the force from the label, not the size.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Length = relative magnitude; a longer arrow is a bigger force, and it tells you the direction of the resultant.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Draws both arrows the same length regardless of size, or can't say which force is bigger from the diagram.

responseLevels.gap: Leaves arrows floating or draws none on a still object; reads no meaning from arrow length or direction.
responseLevels.full: Interprets arrow direction as the way a force acts and length as its relative size (concluding balanced/unbalanced and the resultant), and translates a situation into a correct diagram — arrows attached to and acting ON one object, with a still object shown as balanced forces.
responseLevels.partial: Draws labelled arrows with correct directions and reads a single diagram, but slips on one convention — arrows not clearly on the object, 'still = no forces', or ignoring length as magnitude — interpreting OR drawing, but not both cleanly.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Look at this force diagram of a box being pushed across the floor: a long arrow points right labelled 'push', and a shorter arrow points left labelled 'friction'. What do the lengths and directions of the two arrows tell you about what the box is doing? Then draw the force arrows for a book resting still on a table.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Interpreting: does the child read arrow LENGTH as magnitude and DIRECTION as the way the force acts, concluding motion from the longer arrow? Translating (draw the resting book): the tells are whether arrows are ATTACHED to the object (not floating), act ON the book (not forces the book exerts elsewhere), and that a still book still has forces drawn (balanced, not blank). Floating arrows, only a downward arrow, or 'still = no forces' reveal the representational gap.
